cases.abstract: Exploiting planar symmetry in diffusion-based manipulation requires specifying how gripper poses and action noise transform. We introduce Equivariant Diffusion Policy, grounded in a conditional result: when the expert policy is SO(2)-equivariant and noise transforms like actions, the associated noise predictor is also equivariant. Absolute targets rotate with the scene, whereas relative updates require conjugation because the current pose also rotates; linear representations encode both transformations in the denoiser. The implementation uses a finite rotation subgroup: equivariant encoders produce rotation-indexed observation and action features, a shared temporal U-Net processes corresponding orientations, and an equivariant decoder predicts action noise. Across twelve simulation tasks with 100 demonstrations per task and absolute control, the image model attains 53.7% mean peak success versus 42.0% for the non-equivariant diffusion baseline. Relative-control gains are smaller, and image rotations do not exactly match physical scene rotations. On six physical-robot tasks, the voxel model achieves 80-95% success with 20-60 demonstrations, exceeding a similarly sized non-equivariant policy receiving the same voxel inputs. These comparisons support symmetry-constrained denoising as a useful inductive bias for demonstration-limited manipulation.
cases.results: With 100 demonstrations per task, image-based EquiDiff achieved 53.7% mean peak success across twelve simulation tasks under absolute control, compared with 42.0% for DiffPo-C, which uses the same RGB observations and temporal U-Net backbone. Simulation results report maxima over 50 evaluations during training and are averaged over three seeds. Under relative control, the corresponding averages were 35.4% and 33.3%, showing that the gain depends on the action convention. On hardware, both policies received the same voxel grid and had approximately matched parameter counts: after 40 demonstrations, EquiDiff completed letter alignment in 19 of 20 trials, whereas the non-equivariant baseline completed none. Across all six hardware tasks, EquiDiff achieved 80-95% success. Together, the RGB simulation comparison and matched-voxel hardware comparison support an architectural benefit beyond simply switching to 3D observations, with substantially smaller gains for image-based relative control.

cases.abstract: Robot dataset domains can have high imitation losses because actions differ in scale or are difficult to fit, making raw loss an ambiguous basis for selecting a training mixture. Re-Mix learns reusable domain weights through minimax optimization of excess loss relative to a reference policy, prioritizing domains where the learned policy has not yet matched the reference. Gaussian normalization aligns action scales, action discretization addresses multimodality and outliers, and validation-based early stopping keeps the reference informative rather than allowing near-zero training loss to erase this comparison. Averaged weights then train downstream diffusion policies, separating curation from policy learning without requiring a target task during mixture selection. We evaluate RT-X and Bridge V2 mixtures on physical robots with limited co-training: 25 demonstrations for each of three representative tasks contribute 5% of the training mixture. With 25% of RT-X data retained, Re-Mix reaches 80% reported mean success, compared with 38% for uniform subsetting and 33% for expert-weighted subsetting. Full-data Bridge results are similar under Re-Mix and uniform sampling, whereas the subset comparison favors Re-Mix, showing why full-data weighting and data removal must be evaluated separately.
cases.results: Mixture choice mattered more after subsetting than in the full-data Bridge comparison. With all Bridge data, Re-Mix and uniform sampling produced similar task success; retaining only 25% of the dataset yielded reported mean success of 90% for Re-Mix, 50% for uniform subsetting, and 22% for Self-Supervised Prototypes, which selects trajectories using CLIP image embeddings. At the same retention fraction on RT-X, Re-Mix reached 80%, versus 38% with uniform and 33% with expert-derived subset weights. These contrasts favor the learned weighting procedure over both size-based sampling and visual-diversity selection under the tested data budget, rather than establishing that reweighting always helps. Final diffusion policies shared 400,000 training steps and co-training data comprising 25 demonstrations for each of three representative tasks at 5% mixture weight; evaluation used ten physical executions per task. The findings therefore concern generalization after limited co-training, not zero-shot transfer to the evaluation setups.
